```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 144, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
source("figure-style.R")
library(idiographic)
data(srl)
data(submissions)
```

A regression model of intensive longitudinal data relates an outcome on each
occasion to predictors measured on the same or an earlier occasion. The data
contain many occasions for each of many persons, and the model can be
estimated for the sample as a whole, for groups of persons, or for each
person separately [@lopezpernas2025]. The three levels rest on different
assumptions about how far persons share the same process.

A pooled model, also termed variable-centred, estimates one set of
coefficients from the data of all persons. It assumes that the coefficients
are identical across persons, or that their average is the quantity of
interest. When persons differ in the strength or the direction of an
association, the pooled coefficient describes the average of the sample and
can misdescribe most of its members [@molenaar2004]. A subgroup model, also
termed person-centred, partitions the persons into groups with similar
coefficients and estimates one model per group. It assumes that the
heterogeneity between persons takes the form of a small number of distinct
processes. A person-specific model, also termed idiographic, estimates a
separate model for each person from that person's repeated measures. It
treats each person as a separate system and requires enough occasions per
person to estimate the coefficients with useful precision.

Estimating the three levels on the same data turns these assumptions into
testable claims. The comparison shows whether the person-specific
coefficients spread more than sampling error predicts, whether that spread
forms distinct groups, and how well the pooled coefficient represents the
individual persons. `fit_lm()` estimates linear models, `fit_glm()` estimates
generalized linear models for binary and count outcomes, and the `scope`
argument of both selects the levels.

## Linear models

```{r lm-values, include = FALSE}
n_learners <- length(unique(srl$name))
n_days <- length(unique(srl$day))
# fit_lm() holds out the last ceiling(test_prop * n) occasions of each person,
# with test_prop = 0.2 by default.
test_days <- ceiling(0.2 * n_days)
train_days <- n_days - test_days
```

The example models daily effort as a linear function of efficacy and
monitoring for the `r n_learners` learners in `srl`. `fit_lm()` estimates the
pooled model and one model per learner. Each model is estimated on the first
`r train_days` days of each learner, and the last `r test_days` days are held
out to evaluate predictions, as described in the prediction vignette. The
pooled model combines the occasions of all learners, and occasions of the
same learner are correlated, so its standard errors are clustered on the
learner [@liang1986].

```{r lm-fit}
lm_fit <- fit_lm(srl, y = "effort", x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                 id = "name", time = "day",
                 scope = c("pooled", "individual"))
coefs(lm_fit, scope = "pooled")
```

```{r lm-pooled-values, include = FALSE}
pooled_lm <- coefs(lm_fit, scope = "pooled")
pooled_efficacy <- subset(pooled_lm, term == "efficacy")
pooled_monitoring <- subset(pooled_lm, term == "monitoring")
two_dp <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
three_dp <- \(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
```

In the pooled model, effort increases by `r two_dp(pooled_efficacy$estimate)`
points per point of efficacy (SE = `r three_dp(pooled_efficacy$std_error)`)
and by `r two_dp(pooled_monitoring$estimate)` points per point of monitoring
(SE = `r three_dp(pooled_monitoring$std_error)`), with the other predictor
held constant. These coefficients estimate the average association in the
sample. The person-specific coefficients show whether this average describes
the individual learners.

### Person-specific coefficients

A person-specific model compares the days of one learner with each other, so
its slope estimates the within-person association of that learner. The
individual scope returns one slope per learner.

```{r lm-individual}
coefs(lm_fit, scope = "individual", term = "efficacy", sort_by = "estimate")
```

```{r lm-individual-values, include = FALSE}
person_slopes <- coefs(lm_fit, scope = "individual", term = "efficacy", sort_by = "estimate")
lowest <- head(person_slopes, 1)
highest <- tail(person_slopes, 1)
signed <- \(x) sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
number_word <- \(n) c("No", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six", "Seven", "Eight", "Nine")[n + 1]
n_negative <- sum(person_slopes$estimate < 0)
n_near_pooled <- sum(abs(person_slopes$estimate - pooled_efficacy$estimate) < 0.10)
median_se <- median(person_slopes$std_error)
sd_slopes <- sd(person_slopes$estimate)
```

The person-specific efficacy slopes range from `r signed(lowest$estimate)`
(`r lowest$subject`) to `r signed(highest$estimate)` (`r highest$subject`),
with a median of `r two_dp(median(person_slopes$estimate))`.
`r number_word(n_negative)` of the `r n_learners` learners have negative
slopes, and `r n_near_pooled` have a slope within 0.10 of the pooled value of
`r two_dp(pooled_efficacy$estimate)`. The observed spread of the slopes has
two sources, true differences between learners and sampling error. Each
slope rests on `r train_days` days, and its standard error has a median of
`r two_dp(median_se)` across learners. The standard deviation of the observed
slopes is `r two_dp(sd_slopes)`, `r tolower(number_word(round(sd_slopes / median_se)))`
times the typical standard error, so sampling error accounts for a small
share of the spread.

### Heterogeneity of the coefficients

The separation of true heterogeneity from sampling error is the problem that
random-effects meta-analysis addresses, with persons in the role of studies
[@dersimonian1986]. The model treats each person-specific slope as an
estimate of that person's true slope and the true slopes as draws from a
normal distribution. It estimates the mean of the true slopes, their standard
deviation $\tau$, and the share $I^2$ of the observed variance that reflects
true differences. `pool_coefs()` applies the DerSimonian--Laird estimator to
the person-specific coefficients.

```{r lm-heterogeneity}
pool_coefs(lm_fit)
```

```{r lm-heterogeneity-values, include = FALSE}
pooled_slopes <- as.data.frame(pool_coefs(lm_fit))
re_efficacy <- subset(pooled_slopes, term == "efficacy")
true_range <- re_efficacy$estimate + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * re_efficacy$tau
wb_lm <- fit_within_between(srl, y = "effort", x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                            id = "name", time = "day")
wb_efficacy <- subset(as.data.frame(contextual(wb_lm)), variable == "efficacy")
training_days <- subset(srl, day <= train_days)
efficacy_variance <- aggregate(efficacy ~ name, data = training_days, FUN = var)
slope_variance <- merge(person_slopes, efficacy_variance, by.x = "subject", by.y = "name")
r_slope_variance <- cor(slope_variance$estimate, slope_variance$efficacy)
```

For efficacy, the mean of the true slopes is
`r two_dp(re_efficacy$estimate)` (95% CI `r two_dp(re_efficacy$conf_low)` to
`r two_dp(re_efficacy$conf_high)`), $\tau$ is `r two_dp(re_efficacy$tau)`,
and $I^2$ is `r two_dp(re_efficacy$i2)`, so
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * re_efficacy$i2)` of the observed variance of the
slopes reflects true differences between learners. Under the normal
distribution of the true slopes, 95% of learners have a slope between
`r signed(true_range[1])` and `r signed(true_range[2])`, an interval that
contains learners for whom efficacy and effort are unrelated as well as
learners with a strong positive association.

The mean of the true slopes, `r two_dp(re_efficacy$estimate)`, is smaller
than the pooled coefficient, `r two_dp(pooled_efficacy$estimate)`, for two
reasons. The pooled coefficient also contains the between-person
association, which is the larger of the two for efficacy, and with the
person means separated the pooled within-person slope falls to
`r two_dp(wb_efficacy$within)`, as the section on within-person and
between-person effects shows. The pooled regression also weights each
learner by the within-person variance of efficacy, and learners with more
variable efficacy have steeper slopes (r = `r two_dp(r_slope_variance)`),
whereas the random-effects model weights each learner by the precision of
that learner's slope.

```{r lm-plot, fig.height=6.4, fig.cap="Figure 1. Person-specific efficacy slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the mean of the true slopes, and the shaded band covers the interval expected to contain 95% of the true slopes."}
plot_coefs(lm_fit, term = "efficacy")
```

### Subgroups

Person-centred research assumes that the processes of many persons can be
summarised by a small number of types, each type representing persons who
share the same process. Effort can depend on efficacy for the learners of one
type and on monitoring for the learners of another. When such types exist, a
model per subgroup describes each process more faithfully than the pooled
model and estimates it more precisely than the person-specific models,
because each subgroup combines the occasions of several persons. The
heterogeneity found above can take two forms. The slopes can form distinct
clusters, which supports types, or vary continuously around a single mean,
which supports a single population with individual differences in degree.
Clustering methods return groups in both cases, so the form of the
heterogeneity is tested before any grouping is interpreted [@bauer2003].

`test_subgroups()` compares mixture models with one to four components for
the person-specific slopes of efficacy and monitoring and selects the number
of components by the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), on which lower
values indicate a better balance of fit and complexity. A single component,
the hypothesis of one population, is among the models compared.

```{r lm-subgroups}
subgroup_test <- test_subgroups(srl, y = "effort",
                                x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                                id = "name", time = "day")
subgroup_test
as.data.frame(subgroup_test) |> head()
```

```{r lm-subgroup-values, include = FALSE}
bic_table <- as.data.frame(subgroup_test)
best_one <- min(subset(bic_table, k == 1)$bic)
best_two <- min(subset(bic_table, k == 2)$bic)
one_dp <- \(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
```

The one-component model has the lowest BIC (`r one_dp(best_one)`), and the
best two-component model has a BIC of `r one_dp(best_two)`. The learners in
`srl` therefore form a single population whose slopes differ continuously,
and the person-specific models are the appropriate description of these
differences.

## Generalized linear models

Many outcomes of intensive longitudinal studies are binary or counts, such as
whether a learner submits an assignment on a given day or how many messages a
learner posts. A linear model for such outcomes predicts values outside the
possible range and assumes a constant residual variance, whereas the variance
of a binary or count outcome depends on its mean. A generalized linear model
relates the predictors to a transformation of the expected outcome through a
link function and takes the variance from the distribution of the outcome
[@mccullagh1989]. For a binary outcome, the logistic model relates the
predictors to the log-odds of the outcome, and a slope is the change in
log-odds per unit of the predictor. `fit_glm()` estimates these models at the
same levels as `fit_lm()`, with `family = "binomial"` for binary outcomes,
`"poisson"` for counts, and `"negbin"` for counts whose variance exceeds their
mean.

```{r glm-values, include = FALSE}
sub_learners <- length(unique(submissions$learner))
sub_days <- length(unique(submissions$day))
learner_types <- unique(submissions[c("learner", "type")])
n_engaged <- sum(learner_types$type == "engaged")
n_avoidant <- sum(learner_types$type == "avoidant")
spelled <- \(n) c("Twenty", "Thirty", "Forty", "Fifty")[match(n, c(20, 30, 40, 50))]
```

The `submissions` data are simulated, so that the true process of each
learner is known and the estimates at each level can be compared with it.
`r spelled(sub_learners)` learners are observed on `r sub_days` days, with a
binary record of whether an assignment was submitted. The learners belong to
two types. For the `r n_engaged` engaged learners, the log-odds of submitting
rise with daily motivation, with a slope of 1.2, and for the `r n_avoidant`
avoidant learners they fall, with a slope of −0.6. The slope of each learner
varies around the slope of the type with a standard deviation of 0.15, and
the `type` column records the true type.

```{r glm-data}
head(submissions)
```

### Pooled coefficients

```{r glm-pooled}
pooled_glm <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                      id = "learner", family = "binomial",
                      time = "day", scope = "pooled")
coefs(pooled_glm)
```

```{r glm-pooled-values, include = FALSE}
pooled_motivation <- subset(coefs(pooled_glm), term == "motivation")
p_text <- \(p) sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p))
```

The pooled motivation slope is `r two_dp(pooled_motivation$estimate)`
(SE = `r two_dp(pooled_motivation$std_error)`,
p = `r p_text(pooled_motivation$p_value)`). The pooled model averages two
processes of opposite sign, and its slope describes neither type. A pooled
analysis of these data would conclude that motivation is at most weakly
related to submission, although motivation is strongly associated with
submission for every learner, positively for half of the learners and
negatively for the other half.

### Subgroups

The simulated data contain two types, and the subgroup analysis is expected
to recover them. `find_subgroups()` with `k = "auto"` chooses the number of
subgroups by the same mixture comparison as `test_subgroups()` and assigns
the learners to subgroups by their person-specific slopes. The assignment is
repeated on 30 resamples of the occasions, and the stability of the
partition is the proportion of resamples in which each learner is grouped
with the same learners. Stability measures the reproducibility of a
partition, which is distinct from its validity, since a single continuous
population divided at the same point also yields a stable partition.

```{r glm-subgroups}
set.seed(1)
submission_groups <- find_subgroups(submissions, y = "submitted",
                                    x = "motivation", id = "learner",
                                    time = "day", k = "auto", reps = 30)
submission_groups
```

```{r glm-subgroup-values, include = FALSE}
group_table <- merge(groups(submission_groups), learner_types,
                     by.x = "subject", by.y = "learner")
agreement <- table(group_table$subgroup, group_table$type)
# Each subgroup is labelled by the true type that dominates it.
dominant <- colnames(agreement)[apply(agreement, 1, which.max)]
n_match <- sum(apply(agreement, 1, max))
avoidant_group <- rownames(agreement)[dominant == "avoidant"]
engaged_group <- rownames(agreement)[dominant == "engaged"]
avoidant_in_avoidant <- agreement[avoidant_group, "avoidant"]
engaged_in_avoidant <- agreement[avoidant_group, "engaged"]
engaged_in_engaged <- agreement[engaged_group, "engaged"]
bic_gain <- submission_groups$test$evidence
stability <- mean(groups(submission_groups)$stability)
```

Two subgroups are selected, with a BIC lower by `r one_dp(bic_gain)` than
that of a single population, and the stability of the partition is
`r two_dp(stability)`. The partition matches the simulated types for
`r n_match` of the `r sub_learners` learners. The `r avoidant_in_avoidant`
avoidant learners and `r engaged_in_avoidant` engaged learner form the first
subgroup, and the remaining `r engaged_in_engaged` engaged learners form the
second. The assignment enters `fit_glm()` through the `subgroup` argument, so
that the pooled, subgroup and person-specific models are estimated on the
same data.

```{r glm-all}
glm_fit <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                   id = "learner", family = "binomial", time = "day",
                   scope = c("pooled", "subgroup", "individual"),
                   subgroup = submission_groups)
coefs(glm_fit, scope = "subgroup")
```

```{r glm-subgroup-slopes, include = FALSE}
subgroup_slopes <- subset(coefs(glm_fit, scope = "subgroup"), term == "motivation")
avoidant_slope <- subset(subgroup_slopes, subgroup == avoidant_group)$estimate
engaged_slope <- subset(subgroup_slopes, subgroup == engaged_group)$estimate
glm_persons <- merge(coefs(glm_fit, scope = "individual", term = "motivation"),
                     learner_types, by.x = "subject", by.y = "learner")
avoidant_person_mean <- mean(subset(glm_persons, type == "avoidant")$estimate)
true_type_fit <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                         id = "learner", family = "binomial", time = "day",
                         scope = "subgroup", subgroup = "type")
true_avoidant <- subset(coefs(true_type_fit), term == "motivation" & subgroup == "avoidant")$estimate
```

The subgroup motivation slopes are `r signed(avoidant_slope)` and
`r signed(engaged_slope)`, against generating slopes of −0.6 and 1.2. The
subgroup analysis recovers the two processes that the pooled slope averaged
away. The slope of the avoidant subgroup lies closer to zero for two
reasons. The person-specific slopes of the avoidant learners average
`r signed(avoidant_person_mean)`, and a model fitted to the
`r n_avoidant` avoidant learners alone gives `r signed(true_avoidant)`. The
engaged learner assigned to the avoidant subgroup moves the slope further
toward zero.

### Person-specific coefficients

```{r glm-split-values, include = FALSE}
sub_test_days <- ceiling(0.2 * sub_days)
sub_train_days <- sub_days - sub_test_days
```

The person-specific models estimate the slope of each learner from that
learner's first `r sub_train_days` days, with the last `r sub_test_days`
days held out.

```{r glm-individual}
coefs(glm_fit, scope = "individual", term = "motivation", sort_by = "estimate")
```

```{r glm-individual-values, include = FALSE}
glm_slopes <- coefs(glm_fit, scope = "individual", term = "motivation", sort_by = "estimate")
engaged_person_mean <- mean(subset(glm_persons, type == "engaged")$estimate)
subgroup_se <- sort(subgroup_slopes$std_error)
```

The person-specific slopes range from `r signed(min(glm_slopes$estimate))`
to `r signed(max(glm_slopes$estimate))`. They average
`r signed(avoidant_person_mean)` for the avoidant learners and
`r signed(engaged_person_mean)` for the engaged learners, close to the
generating values, so the person-specific level recovers both processes from
the data of each learner alone. The cost is precision. A logistic slope
estimated from `r sub_train_days` binary observations has a median standard
error of `r two_dp(median(glm_slopes$std_error))`, against
`r two_dp(subgroup_se[1])` and `r two_dp(subgroup_se[2])` for the subgroup
slopes, which combine the days of about `r n_avoidant` learners each.

### Heterogeneity of the coefficients

The random-effects model of `pool_coefs()` summarises the person-specific
slopes by a normal distribution.

```{r glm-heterogeneity}
pool_coefs(glm_fit)
```

```{r glm-heterogeneity-values, include = FALSE}
re_motivation <- subset(as.data.frame(pool_coefs(glm_fit)), term == "motivation")
```

The mean of the true slopes is `r two_dp(re_motivation$estimate)` (95% CI
`r signed(re_motivation$conf_low)` to `r two_dp(re_motivation$conf_high)`),
$\tau$ is `r two_dp(re_motivation$tau)`, and $I^2$ is
`r two_dp(re_motivation$i2)`. The large $\tau$ reflects the distance between
the two types, since the slopes come from a bimodal distribution with modes
near −0.6 and 1.2. The normal distribution places its mean between the two
modes, at a value that describes neither type, as the pooled slope does. The
test of subgroups therefore determines whether the normal summary is
adequate. It suits a single population with continuous differences, as in
`srl`, and misdescribes a population of distinct types, as in `submissions`.

```{r glm-plot, fig.height=6.8, fig.cap="Figure 2. Person-specific motivation slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the mean of the true slopes, and the shaded band covers the interval expected to contain 95% of the true slopes under a normal distribution."}
plot_coefs(glm_fit, term = "motivation")
```

### Assumptions of the models

Each model rests on assumptions about the data. A violated assumption biases
the coefficients or makes their standard errors too small.

Clustered standard errors allow the occasions of one person to be correlated
with each other and assume that different persons are independent. Learners
in the same classroom share the influence of their teacher, so their outcomes
are correlated, and standard errors clustered on the learner then understate
the uncertainty. For such designs, `fit_within_between()` clusters the
standard errors on the classroom through its `cluster` argument, while
`fit_lm()` and `fit_glm()` cluster on the person only.

A person-specific model is estimated from the occasions of one person, so its
precision depends on the number of occasions of that person. A person with
fewer than 10 complete estimation occasions receives no person-specific
model, and `failures()` lists that person with the reason. A binary outcome carries less information per occasion than a
continuous outcome, so a logistic model needs more occasions than a linear
model for the same precision. A person who submits an assignment on every
day, or on none, gives no information about the effect of motivation,
because the outcome never varies.

The family of a generalized linear model states how the variance of the
outcome relates to its mean. The binomial family applies to an outcome with
two values, coded 0 and 1 or as a factor with two levels. The Poisson family
applies to counts whose variance equals their mean. Counts of behaviour
usually vary more than the Poisson family allows, and Poisson standard errors
are then too small. The negative binomial family (`"negbin"`) estimates this
extra variance.

Comparing slopes across persons, as `pool_coefs()` and `find_subgroups()` do,
assumes that every slope is measured in the same unit. This holds when every
person has the same predictors, coded and transformed in the same way. Person
scaling breaks it, because it divides the scores of each person by a
different standard deviation, so a slope of 0.5 means a different change in
raw scores for each person.

## Within-person and between-person effects

A person-specific model estimates the within-person association of each
person, whereas a pooled model of raw scores mixes the within-person and the
between-person association. The within-between model separates the two
associations in one pooled regression. Each predictor is decomposed into the
person mean and the deviation from it, and both components enter the model,
which therefore estimates a within-person slope and a between-person slope
for each predictor [@curran2011; @hoffman2009]. The difference between the
two slopes is the contextual effect, the association of the person mean with
the outcome beyond the association implied by the within-person slope
[@mundlak1978]. The vignette on preparing panel data derives the
decomposition in detail.

```{r wb-fit}
wb_fit <- fit_within_between(srl, y = "effort",
                             x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                             id = "name", time = "day")
contextual(wb_fit)
```

```{r wb-values, include = FALSE}
context_table <- as.data.frame(contextual(wb_fit))
context_table$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(context_table$p_value, method = "BH")
context_efficacy <- subset(context_table, variable == "efficacy")
context_monitoring <- subset(context_table, variable == "monitoring")
p_two <- \(p) sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.2f", p))
```

For efficacy, the within-person slope is
`r two_dp(context_efficacy$within)` and the between-person slope is
`r two_dp(context_efficacy$between)`. The contextual effect of
`r two_dp(context_efficacy$contextual)` (95% CI
`r two_dp(context_efficacy$conf_low)` to
`r two_dp(context_efficacy$conf_high)`,
p = `r p_text(context_efficacy$p_value)`) indicates that learners with a
higher mean efficacy report more effort than their daily relation between
efficacy and effort predicts. For monitoring, the within-person slope is
`r two_dp(context_monitoring$within)` and the between-person slope is
`r two_dp(context_monitoring$between)`, and the contextual effect of
`r signed(context_monitoring$contextual)` (95% CI
`r signed(context_monitoring$conf_low)` to
`r two_dp(context_monitoring$conf_high)`,
p = `r p_two(context_monitoring$p_value)`) is consistent with equal slopes
at the two levels. With two contextual effects tested, the
Benjamini--Hochberg adjusted p-value for efficacy is
`r p_text(context_efficacy$p_adjusted)` [@benjamini1995], and the evidence
for a contextual effect of efficacy is weak.

```{r wb-plot, fig.cap="Figure 3. Within-person and between-person slopes with 95% confidence intervals."}
plot_components(wb_fit)
```

### Assumptions of the decomposition

The decomposition requires variation at both levels. A variable whose person
means are nearly equal has no between-person component to estimate, and a
variable that is constant within every person has no within-person
component. `variance_components()`, described in the vignette on describing
persons, reports the share of variance at each level.

The two slopes differ in what can bias them. The within-person slope compares
occasions of the same person, so any stable characteristic of the person,
measured or unmeasured, cancels from it. Variables that change from day to
day and affect both predictor and outcome, such as sleep or workload, still
bias it. The between-person slope compares persons, and any stable
characteristic that differs between persons and affects the outcome, such as
prior achievement, enters it. The contextual effect inherits this bias, so it
is an association between person means and has no causal interpretation
without further assumptions.

## Choice of level

The level of a regression analysis follows from the research question and
from the evidence about heterogeneity. A question about the average
association in a population is answered by the pooled model, and the
within-between model adds whether that association holds within persons,
between persons, or at both levels. A question about the process of each
person is answered by the person-specific models. Their coefficients are
summarised by the random-effects model when they form a single population,
as in `srl`, and by subgroup models when they form distinct types, as in
`submissions`. The heterogeneity statistics $\tau$ and $I^2$ and the test of
subgroups show which of these descriptions the data support.

Person-specific coefficients estimated from short series are imprecise, and
shrinkage toward the population mean improves their accuracy, as the
vignette on pooling and shrinkage shows with `pool_coefs()` and
`shrink_coefs()`. The prediction vignette evaluates the models on held-out
occasions, and the vignette on subgroups and effects covers subgroup
discovery and heterogeneous treatment effects in detail.

## References
